contentSections: Imagine this. You approve a facade from a small sample on a table and a few renders. Two thousand panels are made. They arrive on site, go up on the building, and under real sunlight the colour looks different, the joints are uneven and a fixing does not line up. Now every panel is wrong, and the schedule is gone. A facade mock-up exists to prevent exactly this. It is a full scale test version of a section of the facade, built and inspected before mass production. This guide explains what a mock-up is, what to test, who signs off and how it saves you money.

What Is a Facade Mock-Up?

A facade mock-up is a full size sample of a representative part of the facade, built with the real materials, finishes, fixings and details planned for the project. It may include a corner, a window, a joint between systems and a floor junction. It is not a small swatch. It is a working preview of the real thing. There are a few levels of preview:

LevelWhat it isPurpose
SampleSmall piece of material or finishCheck colour, texture, feel
Visual mock-upLarger section built for appearanceJudge look, joints, proportion and light
Performance mock-upFull assembly built for testingTest water, air, wind and movement
Site mock-upSection built on the actual buildingCheck installation method and tolerances
Small projects may need only samples and a visual mock-up. Large or complex ones often need performance and site mock-ups too.

Why It Pays for Itself

A mock-up costs money and time. But compare it with the alternative:

• Remaking thousands of panels in a different colour
  • Changing fixings after panels are fabricated
  • Fixing leaks across an entire facade
  • Delaying handover and paying contractors to wait
  • Arguments between the client, designer and installer about who is responsible
One problem found on a mock-up costs a small fraction of the same problem found on the building.
What a Mock-Up Reveals

Colour and Finish

Colour changes with light, angle and surroundings. A panel that looks perfect indoors can look different in strong sun or at dusk. Check the mock-up in morning, afternoon and evening light. Check gloss level and consistency between panels. See our guide on facade colours and finishes.

Joints and Alignment

Joint width, panel flatness and edge quality show up clearly. Hairline joints, in particular, reveal any error. Read about metal cladding joints before you review.

Fixing and Installation

Can installers actually fix the panels as designed? Are brackets reachable? Can a single panel be replaced without removing its neighbours? Mock-ups reveal practical problems that drawings hide.

Water and Weather

A performance mock-up can be tested for water tightness, air leakage and wind pressure. Tests are carried out in a laboratory or on a test rig, following standards agreed for the project.

Interfaces

Facades meet windows, doors, slabs, roofs and other systems. These junctions are where most leaks and visual issues occur. Include at least one typical junction in the mock-up.

Types of Facade Testing

The tests required depend on the project, building height, location and client brief. Common categories include:

• Air permeability. How much air leaks through the system under pressure.
  • Water penetration. Whether water gets through under simulated wind driven rain.
  • Structural and wind load. Whether the system handles design wind pressure and deflection.
  • Thermal movement. How the system handles expansion and contraction.
  • Impact. Resistance to impact where relevant.
  • Fire. Reaction to fire of materials and, where required, assembly behaviour.
  • Finish and coating. Adhesion, thickness, colour and gloss checks.
  • Fixing pull-out. Anchor strength in the actual base material.
Not every project needs every test. Your facade consultant and engineer should define which tests apply and which standards are used.

Who Signs Off?

A mock-up is only useful if someone with authority approves it, and records what was approved. Typical participants:

1. Client or developer. Approves look and quality level.
  2. Architect. Approves design intent, colour, proportions and details.
  3. Facade consultant, if appointed. Checks performance and compliance. See do you need a facade consultant.
  4. Facade contractor or manufacturer. Confirms buildability and production method.
  5. Main contractor. Confirms site interfaces and sequence.
  6. Fire or code consultant, where required.
Record approval in writing, with photographs and a list of any changes asked for. The approved mock-up then becomes the benchmark for production and site quality.
Mock-Up Review Checklist

1. View the mock-up in different light conditions
  2. Check colour and gloss against the approved sample
  3. Measure joint widths and alignment
  4. Inspect corners, edges and returns
  5. Test the fixing method and access for replacement
  6. Check how the facade meets windows, slabs and roofs
  7. Review test results where performance tests were done
  8. List all changes needed, with who is responsible
  9. Get written sign-off before production
  10. Photograph and keep the mock-up as a reference

How Mock-Up Fits in the Facade Process

A typical order is concept design, engineering and shop drawings, mock-up, approval, mass production, delivery and installation. Learn more in how metal facade engineering works and how facade panels are manufactured in India. For a real example of a long, careful process, read from sketch to shimmer.

Timing and Cost

Build the mock-up into the schedule from the start. Allow time for making it, reviewing it, fixing comments and re-checking. Cost depends on size, system and tests required, and is often part of the facade package. Ask your supplier to state clearly whether the mock-up is included, how many rounds of changes are allowed and who pays for testing.
Common Mistakes

• Approving from renders or small samples only
  • Building a mock-up that does not represent the real details
  • Reviewing in poor light or indoors
  • Not recording approvals in writing
  • Changing materials or suppliers after the mock-up is approved
  • Skipping mock-ups to save time, then losing more time later
Frequently Asked Questions

Is a facade mock-up always required?

Not always. Small, simple projects may use samples only. Large, tall or complex facades usually need a full mock-up.

Who pays for the mock-up?

This depends on the contract. Check that your quote states whether the mock-up and testing are included.

How long does a mock-up take?

It depends on the size and complexity of the system. Ask your supplier for a schedule that includes review time.

Can the approved mock-up be used on the building?

Sometimes it is kept as a reference or reused if allowed. Agree this early.

What if the mock-up fails a test?

The design or detail is changed, the mock-up is rebuilt or modified and re-tested before production starts. That is exactly why you build one.
